content_metadata.description: A video analysis focusing on the importance of diversity and inclusion in gamification development, featuring an interview with game designer Jane McGonigal.

qAndA.answer: She is referring to an upcoming event called 'Embracing Inclusion, Driving Innovation' being held on Wednesday night.
qAndA.question: What event is Marilyn Pratt referring to when she mentions 'embracing inclusion'?

qAndA.answer: Jane McGonigal explains that women tend to be turned off by leaderboards because they often prefer collaboration and support over direct competition.
qAndA.question: Why are leaderboards potentially problematic for inclusivity in gamification?

qAndA.answer: Jane points out that one in four gamers is 50 years old or older, highlighting that this demographic might not be as familiar with game mechanics and platforms, requiring consideration in design.
qAndA.question: What is the significance of the age demographic mentioned by Jane McGonigal?

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: So, I'm Marilyn Pratt. I'm a community advocate for the SAP Community Network and I'm here
at the gamification event, the Ino Jam and SAP TechEd Las Vegas 2011. And I was lucky
enough to have a very quick and serendipitous meeting with Jen Garko and I had a question
that I wanted to ask her really in relation to our upcoming event, which is the event called
Embracing Inclusion, Driving Innovation and it is an event that will be held here on Wednesday
night. Inclusion is what I wanted to ask about in the realm of gamification and we have
a kind of thesis around having a more productive outcome, having a more inclusive development
environment. So, I wonder what your experiences are. For sure. As a woman. Yeah, as a different
kind of thing. Yeah, yeah, for sure. So, I mean, of course, I'm very much believer that crowdsourcing
and collective intelligence requires a diversity of participants. I mean, that's just scientifically
back. We know that's true. Theification is particularly interesting because we know
that different kinds of people like different kinds of games or respond to different game
mechanics. So, for instance, men tend to be more engaged by competition, direct competition
against other players. They're also more engaged by leaderboards where they can have sort
of social comparison. Women are very turned off by leaderboards, they see a labor board,
they drop out, they don't like direct competition, they prefer to either cooperate and collaborate
or to just support other people and what they're doing, get positive feedback, give help.
So, that's one thing to think about just from a gender point of view. You don't want to
make a gamification application that's only going to appeal to men because it's really
competitive and point-based leaderboards. You want to think about the women players too.
In terms of age diversity, that's really interesting too because we know that although one
and four gamers are 50 years older older, if you start to get 50 years older, they're
not quite as familiar with games and game platforms. So, it's good to have those members
involved in usability and design and testing. So, you can see, does this actually work for
people who maybe haven't spent 20 hours a week growing out playing games? So, that's
kind of thing that can really be helpful. If you want to make the gamification app that
will engage everybody and that's thinking about the kinds of games people like and their
experience with game platforms can be really helpful.
Thank you guys.
